title: Warehouse and distributed-platform migrations
summary: Three estates, one method: inventory by readers, one disposition per workload, bridges for every cut dependency, each platform in its own vendor's words, three separate equivalences, and a pilot-to-rollback sequence with written tests.
outcomes: Build an inventory from usage evidence and segment workloads into dispositions with drivers and evidence.
Find the dependencies each wave boundary cuts and bridge them with owners and end dates.
Profile legacy, Hadoop and cloud source platforms from each vendor's own documentation, with unknowns kept visible.
Separate loud from silent dialect and engine differences and prove results, performance and permissions separately.
Choose data movement and BI continuity per dataset, set reconciliation depth by risk class, and sequence waves from pilot to rollback.
startingAssumptions: The architecture module has covered target designs, decision records, reconciliation basics and recovery after a switch.
The SQL Server module has shown how one procedure's semantics are decomposed and tested; this module works at the scale of an estate.
Unity Catalog's object model and privileges are familiar from the governance modules.
editorialRationale: Warehouse and distributed-platform migrations fail when a conversion rate is mistaken for progress and a platform is moved as one block, so the module starts from readers rather than objects, segments workloads into dispositions, and turns wave boundaries into explicit bridges before it profiles each source platform in its own vendor's words, with unread cells left unknown. It then separates loud from silent dialect and engine differences, treats results, performance and permissions as three proofs, maps security by persona outcomes, chooses data movement and BI continuity per dataset, and closes with validation depth by risk class, waves, coexistence under a one-writer rule and a pilot-to-rollback sequence with written tests; the enterprise coexistence capstone is where the method is practised at estate scale.

claims.description: Microsoft describes Fabric as a SaaS platform whose workloads, including Power BI, Spark-based data engineering and the Data Warehouse, operate over OneLake, one tenant-wide logical lake on ADLS Gen2; the warehouse separates compute from storage and stores data natively in Delta Lake format; mirroring replicates sources such as Azure Databricks and Snowflake into OneLake; shortcuts give zero-copy access to ADLS, Amazon S3 and Google Cloud Storage; governance uses Microsoft Purview.

claims.description: AWS describes Amazon Redshift as a fully managed, petabyte-scale cloud data warehouse offered as Redshift Serverless or provisioned clusters, in which a leader node plans queries for compute nodes divided into slices, a distribution key places rows on slices, managed storage scales on Amazon S3 independently of compute, and SQL is based on PostgreSQL with important differences.
claims.context: Live page snippets confirmed 2026-09-23; details from AWS's archived source, out of date since June 2023.

claims.description: In Amazon Redshift, permissions belong to the object owner by default, users gain permissions directly or through groups, roles can inherit permissions from other roles, row-level security policies restrict rows and apply to SELECT, UPDATE and DELETE but not to INSERT, COPY or ALTER TABLE APPEND, and dynamic data masking transforms values at query time.
claims.context: Live page titles and snippets confirmed 2026-09-23; details from AWS's archived source, out of date since June 2023.

claims.description: Snowflake describes a self-managed service with a hybrid shared-disk and shared-nothing architecture, a central data repository over massively parallel compute clusters, in three layers: loaded data in an internal optimized, compressed, columnar format reachable only through SQL, virtual warehouses as independent compute clusters, and a cloud services layer that includes access control; access control grants privileges on securable objects to roles, which can be granted to users or other roles, and access is denied unless a grant allows it; multi-cluster warehouses add clusters for concurrent load, which differs from resizing for a slow query.
claims.context: Architecture and access-control pages confirmed by search-result title and snippet 2026-09-23, bodies not fetched; multi-cluster page reviewed 2026-09-19.

claims.description: Google describes BigQuery as a fully managed, serverless platform with no infrastructure to set up or manage, queried with GoogleSQL or Python and secured through Identity and Access Management, whose storage and compute layers operate independently; external tables need permission on both the table and the underlying source, while BigLake tables delegate source access to a connection's service account.
claims.context: Overview confirmed by search-result title and snippet 2026-09-23, body not fetched; external data and BigLake pages reviewed 2026-09-19 and 2026-09-20.

claims.description: HDFS stores files as blocks on DataNodes under one NameNode; files are write-once apart from appends and truncates, with one writer at a time; the design moves computation to the data; permissions follow a POSIX-like owner, group and other model with optional ACLs, and user identity comes from the operating system or Kerberos.
claims.context: Apache Hadoop documentation sources read at the trunk branch; the stable rendered pages confirmed by search 2026-09-23.

claims.description: Spark 3.0 switched to the Proleptic Gregorian calendar, changing results for dates before 15 October 1582, and applies ANSI store assignment on insert, raising an error where Spark 2.4 stored the low-order bits; since Spark 4.0 ANSI mode is on by default and CREATE TABLE without USING no longer defaults to a Hive table; Spark SQL is designed to be compatible with the Hive Metastore, SerDes and UDFs.
claims.context: Open-source Apache Spark migration guide, read at the v4.0.4 tag and cited at the 4.0.2 page; vendor runtimes may set other defaults.

claims.description: In Spark 4.0, ANSI mode is on by default and invalid operator inputs raise runtime errors instead of returning NULL; try_divide returns NULL on a zero divisor; the / operator always performs floating point division, so 3 / 2 is 1.5, while div casts the quotient to long, so 3 div 2 is 1.
claims.context: Open-source Apache Spark, read at the v4.0.4 tag; the div usage text and the ANSI page differ on a zero divisor, so check the behaviour on the target compute.

claims.description: In Spark SQL, when no null ordering is given, NULLs sort first for ascending order and last for descending order.

concepts.definition: Records of which people, reports and jobs actually read each object over a stated window, joined to the catalog to sort objects by reader.
concepts.example: Basalt's 90-day history splits 1,240 tables into 610 read by people or reports, 410 read only by scripts and 220 unread.

concepts.definition: The single decision recorded for a workload: stay, coexist by sharing or federation, migrate in a named wave, retire, or not yet with a dated condition.
concepts.example: Cinderline's finance close marts are 'not yet', reconsidered on 15 February after the year-end close.

concepts.definition: A dependency whose producer and consumer are assigned to different migration waves, so one side runs on each platform after the earlier cutover.
concepts.example: line_health stays on Basalt until wave 2 while the dashboards that read it move in wave 1.

concepts.definition: A temporary path carrying data across a cut dependency, forward into the target or back to the source, with an owner, a freshness target and an end date.
concepts.example: A sync-back feeds Basalt's finance marts from the new quality table until wave 3.

concepts.definition: A table describing a source platform in its own vendor's current documentation: storage, compute, service model, dialect, access control and open-format access, with unread cells marked unknown.
concepts.example: The Fabric column records OneLake and Delta Lake warehouse storage from Microsoft's own overview.

concepts.definition: Hadoop's distributed file system, in which a NameNode manages the namespace and DataNodes store file blocks; files are write-once apart from appends and truncates.
concepts.example: The sensor cluster keeps six years of readings as Parquet and ORC files in HDFS.

concepts.definition: Moving a job to a newer engine release whose documented defaults and semantics differ, such as the calendar, store assignment and ANSI mode.
concepts.example: An insert that stored 257 as 1 under Spark 2.4 raises an error under ANSI store assignment.

concepts.definition: A statement that runs on both engines and returns different results, so neither compilation nor row counts reveal it.
concepts.example: Basalt returns 3 for 7 / 2 while Spark's / returns 3.5.

concepts.definition: Tool-driven translation of source SQL into the target dialect, measured by how much of the code parses and produces output.
concepts.example: 389 of 420 Basalt scripts converted without error in the synthetic assessment.

concepts.definition: The separate proofs a migrated workload needs: the same keyed results, acceptable performance under recorded load, and the same permission outcomes.
concepts.example: 33 of 38 pilot scripts were equal on results, two dashboards missed the response target and one grant widened access.

concepts.definition: A fixed set of queries run as each persona on the source and target paths, comparing allowed or denied access, visible rows and masked values.
concepts.example: The plant 2 supervisor saw only plant 2 on Basalt and every plant after the grants were translated line by line.

concepts.definition: In Unity Catalog, a grant on a catalog or schema can apply to current and future objects beneath it.
concepts.example: A schema-level SELECT lets the contractor group read a table created next week.

concepts.definition: How a dataset reaches the target during migration: copied and kept current, queried in place, shared by its owner, or re-derived from upstream sources.
concepts.example: Pellworth's finance mart is federated while quality history is copied and loaded daily.

concepts.definition: The measures, filters, business rules, refresh mode and identity that together decide a report's numbers, wherever each is defined.
concepts.example: The 06:00 business-day cutoff lived in Basalt's view, not in the dashboard.

concepts.definition: A class set before the run by the consequence of a wrong number, deciding field coverage, tolerances, parallel-run length, performance and permission depth, and sign-off.
concepts.example: The plant-quality mart is class 2: every key and reported field for five clean days.

concepts.definition: A set of workloads that cut over together, with entry conditions, bridges for its cut dependencies and an exit test.
concepts.example: Wave 1 is the plant-quality mart and its 14 dashboards.

concepts.definition: During coexistence each dataset has exactly one path allowed to write it; every other copy is derived, read-only and reconciled against it.
concepts.example: Basalt writes the quality mart until cutover; afterwards the lakehouse does.

concepts.definition: A period in which old and new paths run on the same inputs, the old path still serves users, and results are compared daily at the workload's risk class.
concepts.example: All plants run on both paths and are compared daily until five consecutive clean days.

concepts.definition: An observable condition, written before cutover, that on its own sends users back to the retained old path.
concepts.example: Plant dashboards not ready by 07:30 sends users to the named Basalt fallback.

concepts.definition: The comparison mode of Lakebridge's reconcile command: schema, row (whole-row hash), data (keyed) or all.
concepts.example: A data report on quality_day keyed by inspection_id lists mismatched and missing rows.

concepts.definition: The Gregorian calendar extended backwards before 1582, used by Spark since 3.0 in place of the hybrid Julian and Gregorian calendar.
concepts.example: A 0001-01-01 placeholder written by Spark 2.4 is compared after a newer engine reads it.

concepts.definition: Microsoft Fabric's continuous replication of data from external sources into OneLake.
concepts.example: An Azure Databricks table mirrored into OneLake for a Fabric-based report.

concepts.definition: A database-level rule that limits the rows, or masks the values, a user or role sees at query time.
concepts.example: Pellworth's policy shows each plant manager only that plant's cost rows.

visuals.title: The sensor cluster moves on four tracks
visuals.alt: The sensor cluster moves on four tracks. One cluster couples storage, metadata, compute, permissions and schedules. Each is a separate thing to move.
visuals.caption: Files, table metadata, the engine and permissions each move to a different target part, and the engine change can expose an old defect. Synthetic teaching example.
visuals.textEquivalent:
What the sensor cluster actually holds: One cluster couples storage, metadata, compute, permissions and schedules. Each is a separate thing to move. Nodes: HDFS files: Parquet, ORC. Blocks on DataNodes under one NameNode; write-once, one writer. (selected); Hive metastore: Maps table names and partitions to HDFS paths. (selected); Spark 2.4 jobs: 64. Run on YARN beside the data they read. (selected); Path permissions: Owner, group and other bits plus ACLs on directories. (selected); Workflow scheduler: 30 workflows. Launches jobs in dependency order. (selected). Relationships: Hive metastore → HDFS files: maps tables to; Spark 2.4 jobs → Hive metastore: resolve tables; Path permissions → HDFS files: guard; Workflow scheduler → Spark 2.4 jobs: launches.

Four moves, four target parts: Each track lands on a different part of the target. Two of them change behaviour, not just location. Nodes: Object storage files: Same Parquet and ORC bytes, copied from HDFS and counted. (selected); Unity Catalog tables: Registered from the metastore's names and paths, or federated while both run. (selected); Current Spark runtime: ANSI mode on by default since Spark 4.0; behaviour to test. (warning); Table grants: Directory intent re-expressed per table and group. (warning); Lakeflow Jobs: Workflows rebuilt as tasks with dependencies. (selected). Relationships: Unity Catalog tables → Object storage files: registers; Current Spark runtime → Unity Catalog tables: read tables; Table grants → Unity Catalog tables: grant on tables; Lakeflow Jobs → Current Spark runtime: runs.

The engine change surfaces an old defect: The same insert gives a wrong value under Spark 2.4 and an error under ANSI store assignment. The old number was the defect. Nodes: Scrap-weight job: Inserts a computed weight into a TINYINT column. (selected); Spark 2.4 result: 257 stored as 1. Low-order bits stored silently for years. (warning); Spark 3.0+ result: error. ANSI store assignment rejects the out-of-range value. (selected); Reconciliation: Old and new disagree; the finding goes to the data owner. (pending). Relationships: Scrap-weight job → Spark 2.4 result: under 2.4; Scrap-weight job → Spark 3.0+ result: under 3.0 and later; Spark 2.4 result → Reconciliation: compared; Spark 3.0+ result → Reconciliation: compared.
