questions.prompt: Basalt's catalog lists 1,240 tables. Which evidence justifies treating 220 of them as retirement candidates rather than migration items?

options.text: No read by any person, report or script in 90 days of query history, with each owner asked to confirm.
options.rationale: Usage evidence shows no reader, and the owner's confirmation covers readers the log cannot see.

options.text: The tables have not been modified for more than a year.
options.rationale: Static reference tables can be read every day without changing, so age says nothing about readers.

options.text: The conversion tool could not parse the procedures that create them.
options.rationale: Parsing difficulty describes code complexity, not whether anyone reads the data.

options.text: Each table holds fewer than a thousand rows.
options.rationale: Small lookup tables are often read by every report; size is not usage.

questions.prompt: Wave 1 cuts over the quality mart and the plant dashboards, but no bridge was planned for line_health, which a Spark 2.4 job still writes into Basalt. What happens the morning after cutover?

options.text: The dashboards' line-health panel has no current source on the new path, so it is blank or stale.
options.rationale: The edge from line_health to the dashboards crosses the wave boundary with nothing carrying data across it.

options.text: The Spark 2.4 job fails because Basalt has been switched off.
options.rationale: Basalt keeps running for the finance marts; nothing in wave 1 stops the job writing there.

options.text: The dashboards keep working because BI tools cache every panel indefinitely.
options.rationale: Caches expire and refresh; a cache is not a source and hides the gap only briefly.

options.text: The finance marts stop updating because they read line_health.
options.rationale: Finance reads scrap cost from the quality mart, not line_health; that is the other cut edge.

questions.prompt: A colleague says a sister business on Microsoft Fabric 'keeps its warehouse in a closed format, so everything must be exported before we can read it'. What does Microsoft's own Fabric overview say?

options.text: Fabric Data Warehouse stores data natively in the open Delta Lake format in OneLake, so reading in place is a question to verify, not ruled out.
options.rationale: This is the overview's own statement; access paths, identity and freshness still need checking before a design relies on it.

options.text: Fabric keeps each workspace's data in a separate Azure storage account that the customer provisions.
options.rationale: The overview describes one tenant-wide OneLake and says no Azure account is needed to use Fabric.

options.text: Fabric keeps warehouse tables only inside Power BI reports.
options.rationale: Power BI is one workload over OneLake; the warehouse is its own workload storing Delta Lake tables in OneLake.

options.text: The overview does not describe where Fabric data is stored, so the cell must stay unknown.
options.rationale: It does describe OneLake and the warehouse's Delta Lake storage; unknown is for cells nobody has read.

questions.prompt: After the sensor jobs move from Spark 2.4 to a current runtime, the scrap-weight job fails on an insert that always 'worked'. What does Spark's own migration guide explain?

options.text: Since Spark 3.0, inserts follow ANSI store assignment and reject out-of-range values; Spark 2.4 silently kept the low-order bits, so old rows may already be wrong.
options.rationale: The guide's own example is 257 inserted into a byte column becoming 1 in 2.4; the new error exposes that defect.

options.text: Current runtimes cannot write ORC files, so every insert into an ORC table fails.
options.rationale: Nothing in the guide removes ORC writes; the failure depends on the value's range, not the format.

options.text: The Hive metastore was not migrated, so the table name no longer resolves.
options.rationale: An unresolved table fails analysis on every run with a missing-table error, not only for one value.

options.text: The Proleptic Gregorian calendar changed how integers are stored.
options.rationale: The calendar change affects dates before 15 October 1582, not integer columns.

questions.prompt: Which translated statement is most likely to pass compilation, pass row counts and still change a published number?

options.text: A defect-rate expression dividing two integers, which Basalt truncates and Spark's / computes in floating point.
options.rationale: It runs on both engines, returns the same number of rows and different values; only a keyed value comparison catches it.

options.text: A call to Basalt's DAYS_BETWEEN_BUS function, which the target does not have.
options.rationale: An unknown function fails at compile time, so it is visible before any number is published.

options.text: A division by zero that Basalt answered with NULL.
options.rationale: Under ANSI mode the target raises an error at run time; the failure is loud, not silent.

options.text: A query that reads a table the conversion tool renamed incorrectly.
options.rationale: A missing table fails analysis immediately, which is loud and cheap to find.

questions.prompt: After translation, the contractor group can read a table created last week in the quality schema, although Basalt never allowed it. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: A schema-level SELECT grant in Unity Catalog, which applies to current and future tables, replaced Basalt's per-table grants.
options.rationale: A parent grant reaches tables created later; the per-table source model never did.

options.text: The table was created as an external table, which bypasses Unity Catalog privileges.
options.rationale: External tables are still governed by Unity Catalog privileges; their storage location does not waive them.

options.text: A missing row filter lets the contractors see every plant.
options.rationale: A row filter limits rows inside a table the principal can already read; it does not grant the table.

options.text: The network allows the contractors' IP range.
options.rationale: Network reachability and object privileges are separate checks; reaching the endpoint grants no SELECT.

questions.prompt: After repointing, the plant dashboard's defect rate differs from Basalt's on 3 of 30 days, always near shift changes. What is the best first check?

options.text: Compare the business-day cutoff and exclusions in Basalt's view with the new table's definition, per plant and day.
options.rationale: Differences clustered near shift changes point to a boundary rule that lived in the old view.

options.text: Increase the SQL warehouse size and refresh the dashboard.
options.rationale: Capacity changes speed, not which rows a definition counts; the numbers would stay different.

options.text: Re-run the conversion tool on the dashboard's queries.
options.rationale: The queries converted; the rule that changed the meaning was never in them.

options.text: Accept a 5 percent tolerance because the dates are close.
options.rationale: A tolerance invented after seeing the difference hides a definition change nobody agreed to.

questions.prompt: The migration lead proposes assigning reconciliation classes after the first parallel-run results arrive, 'so we don't over-test tables that already match'. Why does the matrix refuse this?

options.text: The class is set before the run by the consequence of a wrong number; choosing it after seeing results lets the evidence set its own bar.
options.rationale: Setting depth after results invites lowering it wherever differences appear, which defeats the check.

options.text: Classes are assigned by table size, which is known before any run.
options.rationale: Size affects cost, not the consequence of a wrong number; a small table can feed the close.

options.text: Every table must be class 1, so there is nothing to assign.
options.rationale: The matrix exists because uniform depth either wastes effort or under-tests critical data.

options.text: Classes depend on migration difficulty, which only the conversion report shows.
options.rationale: Difficulty is an inventory risk axis; the class records consequence, not effort.

questions.prompt: During wave 1's parallel run, a quality engineer fixes a mislabelled inspection directly in the lakehouse table because 'that is where we are going anyway'. What does the one-writer rule require?

options.text: Undo the edit, apply the correction through Basalt's path, which writes until cutover, and let the lakehouse copy be rebuilt.
options.rationale: Until cutover the old path is authoritative; an edit to the derived copy creates a second writer and a false difference.

options.text: Keep the edit and copy it back to Basalt so both agree.
options.rationale: That makes the lakehouse a writer before cutover and turns the parallel run into two diverging sources.

options.text: Keep the edit; the lakehouse becomes the writer for that one row.
options.rationale: Per-row writers make reconciliation meaningless; writership is per dataset and changes only at cutover.

options.text: Pause reconciliation until cutover so the edit does not count.
options.rationale: Pausing the comparison hides exactly the divergence the parallel run exists to find.

selfQuestions.prompt: Pellworth's security lead now says federated reads from the group workspace are acceptable only for aggregated finance tables, not for row-level supplier prices. Re-place Pellworth's finance mart and say what evidence each resulting row needs.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: Split the workload in two. Aggregated finance tables stay 'coexist: federate', driver security-review, with evidence of a verified connector for that source and version, the list of aggregated objects exposed and the security lead's written scope. Row-level supplier prices become 'stay', or 'not yet' with a dated review, because no approved path exists; their evidence is the security decision itself and the named consumers who asked for the rows.
selfQuestions.reasoning: A disposition applies to a workload that behaves as one unit; when the security answer differs by data, the workload splits and each part carries its own driver and evidence. Keeping the prices on 'not yet' with a date is an equally valid alternative.

selfQuestions.prompt: A proposal says 'the tool converts 93% of your code automatically, so the migration is 93% done'. Write the two or three sentences you would send to the steering group instead, and list the evidence you would attach.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: The conversion figure says 93 percent of scripts parse and produce target SQL; it says nothing about whether they return the same results, meet response targets or expose the same data. Progress is the number of workloads proven equal on keyed results, a performance replay and persona permission tests, currently 33 of the pilot's 38 scripts. Attached: the conversion report, the reconciliation results with the five open differences and owners, the replay timings and the persona matrix.
selfQuestions.reasoning: It keeps the tool's figure but relabels it as syntax coverage and replaces 'done' with the three equivalences the group needs; any wording that separates conversion from proof is acceptable.

selfQuestions.prompt: Pellworth's finance mart is federated today. The group now wants the month-end close to use Pellworth figures at 06:00 even when Pellworth's warehouse is down for overnight maintenance. Which movement option changes, what writer question appears, and what would you reconcile?
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: Federation cannot serve 06:00 while the source is down, so the close needs a copy: an incremental load of the finance tables into the lakehouse after Pellworth's month-end run, labelled with its as-of time. Pellworth stays the only writer and the copy is read-only on the target. Reconcile keyed rows and totals between Pellworth and the copy after every load, as a class 1 dataset because it feeds the close.
selfQuestions.reasoning: Only a copy decouples readers from source downtime; the writer stays single, and money sets class 1 depth. Change-data-capture replication instead of nightly loads is an acceptable alternative when the lag must be shorter.

selfQuestions.prompt: Wave 2 now ends two weeks before the year-end blackout with no slack. List the two options you would put to the steering group, the evidence for each, and what you would not do.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: Option one: descope wave 2 to the sensor files and tables and move the Spark job upgrade after the blackout; the evidence is the dependency map showing line_health can stay bridged by a forward read until then. Option two: keep the full scope with a hard go or no-go date one week before the blackout and the rollback rehearsal already done. I would not start a cutover inside the blackout or shorten wave 1's clean-day count to win back time.
selfQuestions.reasoning: Both options keep the blackout fixed and the evidence gates intact; the choice trades scope against risk and belongs to the steering group. Other splits of wave 2 are fine if every cut edge keeps a bridge.

selfQuestions.prompt: Write the exit test for the pilot and for the parallel run, the entry conditions for cutover, and three rollback triggers for Cinderline's plant-quality wave, each so that a tired operator could check it.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: Pilot exit: for plant 1 over one week, every key and reported field equal, persona tests identical, and the differences accepted in writing by the quality lead. Parallel-run exit: five consecutive clean days for all plants at class 2, dashboard p95 under 10 seconds on the replay, and rollback rehearsed within 30 minutes. Cutover entry: those records, a named operator and backup, and users told the fallback link. Triggers: dashboards not ready by 07:30; a keyed difference outside the exception register; an access anomaly reported by security.
selfQuestions.reasoning: Each condition names a number, a time or a person, so it can be checked without judgement at 07:00; other thresholds are acceptable if they are stated before the run and owned.

beats.title: Count readers before you count tables
beats.outcome: Build an estate inventory from usage evidence and separate migration candidates, script-only intermediates and retirement candidates.
beats.explanation: An inventory that lists every object treats all 1,240 of Basalt's tables as work. Join the catalog to 90 days of [[dbxfe-warehouse-migration-usage-concept|usage evidence]] instead: which tables a person or report read, which only scheduled scripts read, and which nobody read. Notice in the second state that 220 tables and 25 reports have no reader, so they become retirement candidates for their owners to confirm, not migration items. The third state keeps what logs cannot see, such as dynamic SQL and desktop extracts, as named gaps.

samajh.text: Ghar shift karte waqt koi almirah ke har kapde ko gin ke truck nahi bulata. Pehle dekhte ho ki saal bhar mein kaunse kapde pehne gaye, kaunse bas doosre kapdon ke saath tah kiye pade rahe, aur kaunse kabhi nikle hi nahi. Na pehne hue kapde donate karne se pehle ghar walon se poochte ho, kyunki Diwali wala kurta saal mein ek hi baar nikalta hai.
samajh.mapping: The wardrobe is the catalog, clothes worn this year are tables with readers, clothes that only travel with others are script-only intermediates, and asking the family is owner confirmation.
samajh.boundary: You can see every garment, but a query log can miss readers entirely, such as dynamic SQL or desktop extracts; an unknown reader is a gap, not a zero.

beats.hint: Ask who reads each object, not whether it exists.

handbook.markdown:
**What the inventory is for.** An estate inventory answers one question at the end: what must move, in what order, to keep which promises. The Migration inventory field guide holds the template; this beat is the evidence behind it.

**Start from usage, not from the catalog.** Pull the source platform's query history for a window long enough to include its cycles, then join it to the object catalog. Classify each table: *read by a person or report* (a migration candidate with a consumer), *read only by scheduled scripts* (an intermediate that moves with its producer and consumer, or is designed away), *no reader* (a retirement candidate). Each platform exposes query history through its own system views and retention rules; find the documented one for the source and version instead of assuming a name.

**Worked numbers (synthetic).** Basalt's 1,240 tables split 610 / 410 / 220; 25 of 96 reports were not opened in 90 days. Retirement is still a decision: archive each table's definition and a final copy, ask each owner, and drop nothing until the owner agrees and a recovery window has passed.

**What usage evidence misses.** Dynamic SQL that builds table names at run time, extracts copied to desktops or other systems, annual and audit jobs outside the window, and service accounts shared by several applications. List each as a gap with an owner: an unknown reader is not the same as no reader.

**What to inspect.** The query log's retention, whether it records the end user or only a shared service account, and whether reads through views are attributed to the base tables. On the target, Unity Catalog lineage becomes dependency evidence for supported operations once workloads run there, with its own documented coverage limits.

**Demonstrate honestly.** Show the three counts and the gap list, never a single 'tables to migrate' total.

beats.recap: Join the catalog to usage: readers, script-only intermediates, no-reader candidates and named gaps.

beats.title: Every workload gets one disposition, one driver and its evidence
beats.outcome: Place each workload in stay, coexist, migrate in a wave, retire or not yet, and name the driver and evidence behind it.
beats.explanation: Segment by workload, not by platform: a finance close mart and a plant dashboard on the same appliance face different risks. Each workload gets one [[dbxfe-warehouse-migration-disposition-concept|disposition]] (stay, coexist by sharing or federation, migrate in a wave, retire, or not yet), one driver that decided it, and the evidence needed before anyone treats it as agreed. Notice in the second state that the finance marts are 'not yet' with a dated condition and Pellworth's warehouse coexists: a mixed result is the normal outcome, not a failure.
beats.hint: Ask what would have to be true for this row to be agreed.

handbook.markdown:
**Why segment.** One disposition for a whole platform hides the differences that decide risk. Segment by workload: a set of jobs, tables and consumers that deliver one outcome together. Record its type as well (batch SQL, interactive BI, Spark batch, file export, streaming), because each type lands on a different target component and needs different validation.

**The dispositions** match the coexistence capstone's. *Stay*: nothing changes this period. *Coexist, share*: data stays owned where it is and is made available through recipient-scoped, revocable sharing. *Coexist, federate*: queried in place, read-only, from the other estate. *Migrate in a wave*: moves with an owner, a reconciliation gate, a rehearsal and a rollback. *Retire*: switched off because evidence shows no reader. *Not yet*: deferred with a specific, dated and owned condition.

**Drivers** say why: contract, blackout, dependency, security review, BI continuity, latency, residency, cost or no consumer. One driver per row keeps the argument honest; when two drivers conflict, the row is a decision for its owner, not a spreadsheet formula.

**Worked example (synthetic).** Basalt's support renewal is the reason to move at all, but only the plant-quality mart meets the pilot criteria. The finance close marts wait for the year-end close; Pellworth's Redshift warehouse coexists until its security team has reviewed cross-company access.

**When not to migrate.** A workload with no consumer, a contract that forbids change or a blackout window is a reason to stay, retire or wait, not a failure of the plan.

**What to inspect.** Rows whose evidence column is empty, and rows whose disposition depends on an unknown in the platform profile: neither can be final.

beats.recap: One workload, one disposition, one driver, and the evidence that would make it agreed.

beats.title: A wave boundary that cuts a dependency needs a bridge
beats.outcome: Find the dependencies a wave boundary cuts and give each a bridge with a direction, an owner and an end date.
beats.explanation: Draw jobs, tables and reports as a graph, then colour wave 1. Every edge between a wave-1 node and a node that stays behind is a [[dbxfe-warehouse-migration-cut-concept|cut dependency]]: on cutover day one side reads from, or writes to, a platform the other has left. Notice in the second state that the plant dashboards still read line_health from Basalt, and the finance marts still read scrap cost from Basalt's quality mart. The third state gives each cut a [[dbxfe-warehouse-migration-bridge-concept|bridge]], a forward read or a dated sync-back, with an owner and an end.

samajh.text: Socho city ka bus depot naye stand pe shift ho raha hai, par pehle mahine sirf aadhe routes jaayenge. Jo bhi route purane stand ke kisi stop se judta hai, uske liye ek feeder bus chahiye, jiska time-table aur band hone ki tareekh pehle se tay ho. Bina feeder ke, jo log purane stop pe utarte hain, woh naye stand tak pahunch hi nahi paate.
samajh.mapping: Routes are dependency edges, the new stand is the target platform, feeder buses are bridges, and their closing dates are the bridges' end dates.
samajh.boundary: A missing feeder bus is noticed at once, while a missing data bridge can leave a panel silently stale; every bridge needs a freshness check as well as a schedule.

beats.hint: Look for edges whose two ends land in different waves.

handbook.markdown:
**Mechanism.** A dependency graph has jobs, tables, files and reports as nodes and reads or writes as edges. Assign each node a wave. An edge whose ends sit in different waves is cut: after the earlier wave cuts over, one end runs on the target and the other on the source. Every cut edge needs one of three answers: move both ends together, bridge the edge for a stated period, or change the design so the edge disappears.

**Two bridge directions.** A *forward bridge* lets a migrated consumer read a producer that has not moved yet: a federated read, which is read-only and depends on a supported connector, or a nightly copy of line_health into the lakehouse. A *backward bridge* feeds a consumer left behind from a producer that has moved: a sync-back of the new quality table into Basalt for the finance marts. Backward bridges write into the old platform, so they need the same reconciliation as the main path and an explicit end date; they are the ones most likely to become permanent by accident.

**Where edges hide.** Cross-database queries, a job on one platform writing into another (line_health), file drops, BI extracts and spreadsheets that query a table by name. Query history finds reads; scheduler definitions find writes; interviews find the spreadsheets.

**Worked example (synthetic).** Wave 1 moves the quality mart and dashboards. The line_health edge gets a forward bridge until wave 2; the scrap-cost edge gets a backward bridge until the finance marts move. Both bridges have an owner in the wave plan.

**What fails.** A cut found on cutover day: a dashboard panel goes blank, or the finance close reads a table that stopped updating yesterday.

**What to inspect.** Every edge crossing a wave line, and each bridge's owner, direction, freshness target and end date.

beats.recap: Colour the waves, find every edge that crosses a wave line, and bridge it with an owner and an end.

beats.title: Read each source platform in its own vendor's words
beats.outcome: Build a platform profile from each vendor's own documentation and keep every unread cell marked unknown with an owner.
beats.explanation: Before mapping anything, profile each source the way its own vendor describes it: where data rests, the compute unit, the service model, the SQL dialect, access control and open-format access. Notice in the second state that Microsoft's overview says Fabric's warehouse stores Delta Lake tables, AWS's archived text puts Redshift storage in a managed tier on S3, and Snowflake's dialect cell stays unknown because no page read here names it. A [[dbxfe-warehouse-migration-profile-concept|platform profile]] never guesses: each unread cell becomes an owned question.
beats.hint: Where did the value in each cell come from, and when?

handbook.markdown:
**Why a profile first.** A migration maps source behaviour onto target behaviour. If the source side of that map is filled from memory, every later decision inherits the error. Read each vendor's own current documentation, record the date and how it was read, and leave unread cells unknown. The coexistence capstone's three-cloud matrix applies the same rule: a cell filled from memory is still unknown.

**What the vendors' own pages say** (every title and snippet confirmed by search on 2026-09-23, no page body fetched; the source panel records how each was read):
- *Snowflake*, from its listing and an earlier reading: a self-managed service with a hybrid shared-disk and shared-nothing design, a central repository over massively parallel compute clusters; as previously read, three layers (database storage, query processing in virtual warehouses, cloud services) with loaded data in an internal compressed columnar format reachable only through SQL. Its access-control overview grants privileges on securable objects to roles, which can be granted to users or other roles. Its multi-cluster page separates adding clusters for concurrency from resizing for one slow query.
- *Microsoft Fabric*, read from Microsoft's page source dated March 2026: a SaaS platform whose workloads, including Power BI, Spark-based data engineering and the warehouse, work over OneLake, one tenant-wide logical lake on ADLS Gen2; the warehouse stores Delta Lake tables natively; Fabric IQ is labelled preview.
- *BigQuery*, from its listing and an earlier reading: fully managed with no infrastructure to manage, queried with GoogleSQL or Python, secured through IAM, with storage and compute layers that operate independently; external tables need permission on the table and on the underlying source, while BigLake delegates source access to a connection.
- *Amazon Redshift*, live titles and snippets confirmed, details from AWS's archived source (out of date since June 2023): Serverless or provisioned clusters, a leader node planning work for compute nodes split into slices, distribution keys placing rows, managed storage on S3, and SQL based on PostgreSQL with important differences.

**Legacy appliances and Hadoop estates** get the same rows, read from the appliance vendor's manuals and the Apache project pages; the next beat profiles the Hadoop estate.

**Neutrality.** The profile describes; it does not rank. No row says faster or cheaper, and no cell is filled from a competitor's comparison.

**What to inspect.** The date and reading method of each cell, and every unknown without an owner.

beats.recap: Profile each source from its own vendor's current pages; unread cells stay unknown and get owners.

beats.title: A Hadoop estate moves as files, metadata, engine and permissions
beats.outcome: Separate the four tracks a Hadoop-to-lakehouse move changes and name the test for each.
beats.explanation: The sensor cluster is not one thing to move. [[dbxfe-warehouse-migration-hdfs-concept|HDFS]] holds Parquet and ORC files as blocks on DataNodes, the Hive metastore maps table names to paths, Spark 2.4 jobs read through it, and path permissions decide who reads which directory. Notice in the second state that each maps to a different target part: object storage, Unity Catalog tables, a current Spark runtime and table grants. The third state shows why the [[dbxfe-warehouse-migration-engine-concept|engine version change]] is its own risk: an insert that stored 257 as 1 under Spark 2.4 now raises an error.
beats.hint: List what changes behaviour, not only what changes location.

handbook.markdown:
**Four tracks, not one move.** A Hadoop estate couples storage, metadata, compute and security on one cluster. HDFS keeps files as blocks on DataNodes under a NameNode, with write-once files and one writer at a time, and was designed to move computation to the data. A lakehouse separates those parts, so each moves on its own track:

1. *Files*: copy Parquet and ORC directories to cloud object storage and verify file counts, bytes and row counts per partition.
2. *Metadata*: register tables and partitions in Unity Catalog, or read the metastore through catalog federation while both estates run; federation is read-only, and the options for a given metastore version need verifying.
3. *Engine*: rerun each job on a current Spark runtime. Spark's own migration guide lists what changed: since 3.0 the Proleptic Gregorian calendar replaces the hybrid calendar for dates before 15 October 1582 and inserts follow ANSI store assignment; since 4.0 ANSI mode is on by default and `CREATE TABLE` without `USING` no longer creates a Hive table. Spark SQL remains designed to work with Hive metastores, SerDes and UDFs.
4. *Permissions*: HDFS applies POSIX-like owner, group and other bits with optional ACLs, and takes identity from the operating system or Kerberos. Re-derive who should read which table and express it as Unity Catalog grants; a directory mode has no one-to-one translation.

Schedules are a fifth, simpler track: rebuild workflows as jobs with explicit dependencies.

**Worked example (synthetic).** One job computed scrap weight into a TINYINT column. Under Spark 2.4, 257 was stored as 1; under ANSI store assignment the insert fails. Reconciliation will show a difference, and the old value is the defect: record it as a finding for the data owner, not a migration error to suppress.

**What to inspect.** Spark and Hive versions, table formats and SerDes, files written by old engines with dates before 1582, and jobs that rely on NULL results for invalid input.

**When not to move a job yet.** When its output has no reader, or its owner cannot explain a difference the engine change exposes.

beats.recap: Files, metadata, engine and permissions move on separate tracks, each with its own test.

beats.title: The dangerous dialect differences compile cleanly
beats.outcome: Classify dialect differences as loud or silent and name the check that catches each silent one.
beats.explanation: A missing function fails at compile time and costs an afternoon. The expensive differences are [[dbxfe-warehouse-migration-silent-concept|silent]]: the same statement runs on both engines and returns different answers. Notice in the first state that Basalt SQL, the fictional appliance's documented behaviour, returns 3 for 7 / 2 while Spark's / always divides in floating point and returns 3.5, and that NULL reject codes sort to opposite ends. The second state classifies each row and names what catches it: the compiler, a first run, or a keyed reconciliation.
beats.hint: Which rows would a row count never notice?

handbook.markdown:
**Three classes.** *Loud at compile*: the target rejects the statement (an unknown function, unsupported syntax). *Loud at run time*: it compiles but fails on some data (division by zero under ANSI mode). *Silent*: it runs and returns a different answer. Conversion effort flows to the first class because it is visible; risk sits in the third.

**Documented target behaviour.** Apache Spark 4.0.4 has ANSI mode on by default: invalid operator inputs raise errors instead of returning NULL, and `try_divide` returns NULL instead of failing on a zero divisor. Its `/` always performs floating point division (`3 / 2` is 1.5), while `div` casts the quotient to long (`3 div 2` is 1). Without an explicit null ordering, ascending sorts put NULLs first. Check the settings in force on the target compute; a vendor runtime can differ from open-source Spark.

**Worked example (synthetic Basalt behaviour).** Basalt truncates integer division, returns NULL for a zero divisor and sorts NULLs last. A defect-rate expression `defects * 100 / inspected` translated unchanged moves from 3 to 3.5 on some rows. Decide what the business meant, then write it explicitly:

```sql
-- Basalt (fictional): 7 / 2 = 3, 5 / 0 = NULL, NULLs sort last
SELECT plant,
       defects * 100 div inspected            AS pct_truncated,
       try_divide(defects * 100.0, inspected) AS pct_or_null
FROM quality_day
ORDER BY reject_code ASC NULLS LAST;
```

Use `div` only if truncation was intended, an exact decimal if not, and `try_divide` only where NULL for a zero denominator is the agreed rule.

**Other silent families to list per source:** string comparison and collation, time zones and timestamp types, empty string against NULL, decimal rounding, implicit casts, and physical DDL such as distribution and sort keys, which do not translate and are chosen again for the target.

**What to inspect.** Every division, sort, string equality and timestamp in the pilot's code, each covered by a keyed reconciliation that would expose a changed value.

beats.recap: Loud differences cost time; silent ones cost trust. Find the silent ones with keyed value checks.

beats.title: A conversion rate measures syntax, not equivalence
beats.outcome: Explain what an automated conversion report shows, quote a tool's status honestly, and name the three equivalences it cannot establish.
beats.explanation: [[dbxfe-warehouse-migration-conversion-concept|Automated conversion]] tools read source code and emit target SQL, and their reports count how much converted. Notice in the first state that 389 of 420 Basalt scripts converted without error, 92.6 percent. The second state puts the pilot's 38 converted scripts through three different tests: five returned different keyed results, two dashboards missed their response target and one grant widened access. Conversion never proves the [[dbxfe-warehouse-migration-equivalence-concept|three equivalences]] of results, performance or permissions; the third state quotes the tool's own status labels.

samajh.text: Landlord ka notice Hindi mein aaya aur aapne phone ki translation app se use English mein badal diya. Grammar ekdum saaf, har line translate ho gayi, lekin 'lock-in period' ka matlab 'notice period' ban gaya. App yeh nahi batati ki matlab badal gaya; woh bas itna dikhati hai ki har shabd ka kuch na kuch ban gaya. Matlab check karne ke liye koi aisa chahiye jo dono bhashayein aur contract samjhe.
samajh.mapping: The translation app is the transpiler, grammatical output is code that compiles, and the person who checks the meaning is reconciliation with a data owner.
samajh.boundary: A query's meaning can be tested exhaustively against data, which a legal translation cannot; reconciliation gives stronger evidence than any reading of the code.

beats.hint: Which of the three equivalences does a conversion report measure?

handbook.markdown:
**What conversion does.** A transpiler parses source SQL and emits target SQL; an analyzer reads a code base and reports object counts, complexity and dependencies. Both help with sizing and with the loud class of dialect differences. Neither runs the result against real data, compares it with the source's answers, times it under real concurrency or checks who can read what.

**The vendor's own framing.** Databricks' warehouse-migration page says most workloads, queries and dashboards can run with minimal code refactoring once the initial data migration and governance configuration are complete. Read that as the claim the pilot tests, workload by workload, not as a result to report.

**Lakebridge, as read in this build.** Lakebridge is Databricks Labs' migration toolkit; its documentation describes analyze, transpile and reconcile steps. Release 0.15.2 on PyPI, uploaded on 10 September 2026, was read directly: it is classified *Development Status 4 - Beta*; its README says it is provided for exploration only, AS-IS, without formal Databricks support SLAs; its command-line code defines `analyze`, `transpile`, `llm-transpile`, `reconcile` and `aggregates-reconcile`, and labels both reconcile commands experimental. Quote those labels and re-check them for the release you use.

**Three equivalences, three tests.**
- *Results*: keyed reconciliation on an aligned basis, at the depth the validation beat sets.
- *Performance*: replay recorded production queries at recorded concurrency and compare latency percentiles against an agreed target; one fast query proves little.
- *Permissions*: run the persona test matrix and compare allowed, denied and visible rows.

**Worked numbers (synthetic).** 389 of 420 scripts converted. Of the pilot's 38, five produced different keyed values (three integer divisions, one NULL ordering, one hand-rewritten business-day function), two dashboards exceeded a 10-second p95 target on the replay, and one translated schema grant exposed a new table to a contractor group.

**How to explain it.** '92.6 percent converted' is a statement about syntax. The statement a steering group needs is '33 of 38 pilot scripts are proven equal on results; here are the five differences and their owners.'

**When a tool helps most.** Sizing, dependency extraction and repeatable reconciliation runs, with every output checked by a person who owns the meaning.

beats.recap: Conversion counts syntax; results, performance and permissions each need their own proof.

beats.title: Map who may see what, then prove it by outcomes
beats.outcome: Translate a source security model by intent and verify it with a persona outcome test.
beats.explanation: Security models differ in shape: Basalt used view-based row security and per-table grants, HDFS uses path permissions, and Redshift has roles, row-level security and masking. Translating GRANT statements line by line maps syntax, not intent. Build a [[dbxfe-warehouse-migration-persona-concept|persona test]] instead: for each persona and object, record what the source allows, then run the same queries on the target. Notice in the first state that two outcomes widened, one through a dropped view and one through [[dbxfe-warehouse-migration-inheritance-concept|privilege inheritance]] from a schema grant to future tables.
beats.hint: Compare what each persona sees, not what each GRANT says.

handbook.markdown:
**Intent before syntax.** A security model has principals (users, groups, roles, service accounts), securables (databases, schemas, tables, paths, columns), grant paths (direct, through groups, through role inheritance) and policies (row rules, masks). Write the intent as a table of persona, object and allowed outcome before converting any GRANT.

**Source shapes differ.** Basalt (fictional) filters plant rows through views and grants table by table. HDFS applies owner, group and other permissions with optional ACLs to paths, with identity from the operating system or Kerberos, so access follows directories rather than tables. Amazon Redshift, in AWS's archived developer guide, grants to the owner by default, adds permissions through groups and roles (roles can inherit from other roles), and offers row-level security policies and dynamic data masking. Microsoft describes Fabric's governance as permissions, sensitivity labels and auditing through Microsoft Purview. BigQuery external tables need permission on the table and on the underlying source.

**Target shape.** In Unity Catalog, reading a table needs SELECT plus USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA on its parents, and a grant on a parent can be inherited by current and future children. Row filters and column masks are evaluated at query time for the querying principal. So a schema-level grant that reproduces 'the contractor group reads the quality schema' also covers every table created there later, which Basalt's per-table grants never did.

**The persona test.** For each persona, run a fixed set of queries on both paths and compare allowed or denied, row counts and masked values. Run it after every grant change, not once. A difference is either an intent decision, recorded with who approved it, or a defect.

**Identity mapping.** Shared logins become named service principals and groups come from the identity provider. Account-level identity design belongs to the identity module; this beat checks outcomes.

**What to inspect.** Views that exist only for security, schema-level grants, role inheritance chains and every persona whose target outcome is wider.

beats.recap: Write the intent as persona outcomes, translate, then prove the outcomes match.

beats.title: Choose data movement per dataset by freshness, writer and failure
beats.outcome: Choose copy, federation, sharing or re-derivation for each dataset and predict how each behaves when its source fails.
beats.explanation: [[dbxfe-warehouse-migration-movement-concept|Data movement]] is chosen per dataset, not per migration. A copy plus incremental loads keeps yesterday's numbers when the source is down; federation reads in place, read-only, and fails with its source; a governed share keeps the owner as writer and can revoke future access. Notice in the second state what happens when each dataset's own source is unavailable for a day: the federated Pellworth finance mart fails, the copied quality history stays readable but a day stale, and shared supplier data follows its provider.
beats.hint: Ask what each consumer needs when the source is down.

handbook.markdown:
**Four options.**
- *Copy, then keep it current*: a bulk historical load (export to open files, load, verify), then incremental loads from query-based extracts or change-data capture. Lakeflow Connect's documented connector categories include CDC database ingestion, files, streaming and query-based ingestion, and source support differs by connector. A copy survives a source outage but lags it.
- *Federate*: query the source in place. Query federation pushes work to the external database, catalog federation reads external object storage with Databricks compute, and both are read-only. Nothing lags, but every query depends on the source's availability, capacity and network path.
- *Share*: the owner grants recipients access and can revoke future access, although revocation does not erase copies a recipient already made.
- *Re-derive*: rebuild the dataset on the target from upstream sources, as line_health will be rebuilt from the sensor files in wave 2.

**The writer question.** For every dataset, name the single writer while both platforms run. A copy has one writer upstream; a federated view has no writer on the target; a share keeps the provider as writer. Two writers is the design error the coexistence beat forbids.

**Worked example (synthetic).** Quality history: a bulk copy of six years, then daily loads from Basalt until cutover, after which the new pipeline writes. Sensor files: copied, then appended nightly. Pellworth's finance mart: federated while it coexists. Supplier master: shared from the group to Pellworth.

**Failure behaviour.** Copies go stale; federated queries fail; shares depend on the provider. Choose per dataset by what its consumers can tolerate, and write the choice and its failure behaviour into the runbook.

**What to inspect.** Egress and network paths, the load that federated queries put on the source, the lag of each copy, and who can revoke each share.

beats.recap: Copies lag, federation fails with its source, shares stay the owner's: choose per dataset.

beats.title: Repointing a report is not moving its meaning
beats.outcome: Find where a report's meaning lives and prove parity per grain before switching its users.
beats.explanation: A dashboard's number depends on more than its connection. [[dbxfe-warehouse-migration-meaning-concept|Report meaning]] lives in measures in the BI model, filters and business rules in the views it reads, extract schedules and the identity it runs as. Notice in the first state that repointing the plant dashboard from Basalt's view to the new table changes its defect rate, because the 06:00 business-day cutoff and the test-lot exclusion lived in Basalt's view. The second state moves those rules into one governed definition and compares totals per plant and day before any user switches.

handbook.markdown:
**Where report meaning lives.** Four places: measures and calculated fields in the BI model; business rules inside the views or procedures the report reads; the refresh mode (live query or scheduled extract) and its schedule; and the identity it runs as, which decides what row-level rules apply. Repointing a connection moves none of them.

**Continuity steps.**
1. For each report in the wave, list its dataset, measures, source views and the rules those views apply.
2. Move rules out of hidden views into one governed definition on the target. Databricks documents metric views, which define a measure once, separately from the dimensions used to group and filter it, and SQL warehouses serve BI tools; a governed view is an acceptable alternative where metric views are not used.
3. Map the refresh identity: shared logins become named service principals, and row filters are tested for the principal that will actually run the query.
4. Prove parity: compare the report's totals per grain (plant and day) over the parallel run, and trace each difference to a rule instead of averaging it away.
5. Switch users only at cutover, keep the old report reachable and clearly named as the fallback, and schedule extracts after the new pipeline completes.

**Worked example (synthetic).** The plant dashboard differed on 3 of 30 days. Basalt's view counted an inspection at 05:40 on the previous business day and excluded test lots; the new table used the calendar day and included them. After both rules moved into one definition, all 30 days matched.

**What fails.** A report certified on Basalt and silently treated as certified on the target; an extract that refreshes before the new pipeline finishes; a row rule that depended on the shared login.

**What to inspect.** Reports with logic in the BI tool, extracts copied to desktops, and refresh times against pipeline completion.

beats.recap: Move the rules, the refresh identity and the schedule with the report, and prove parity per grain.

beats.title: Validation depth follows the cost of a wrong number
beats.outcome: Assign each workload a reconciliation risk class before the run and apply that class's checks.
beats.explanation: Not every table needs the same proof, but the choice must be made before results arrive and by consequence, not effort. A [[dbxfe-warehouse-migration-riskclass-concept|risk class]] records what a wrong number would cost: money or regulation, operational decisions, or exploration. Notice in the first state that every class writes the basis first and compares every key; the classes differ in field coverage, tolerances, parallel-run length, performance and permission checks, and who signs. The second state applies the matrix to three workloads and shows where the pilot stands.

samajh.text: Sabzi wale se bees rupaye wapas lete waqt aap bas ek nazar daalte ho aur note gin lete ho. Par flat ke kaagzaat sign karne se pehle har naam, har number aur har page padhte ho, aur kisi jaankar se bhi padhwaate ho. Farak yeh nahi ki kaam kitna mushkil hai; farak yeh hai ki galti ki keemat kitni hai. Aur kitni jaanch hogi, yeh kaagaz dekhne se pehle tay hota hai.
samajh.mapping: The change from the vegetable seller is a class 3 table, the flat papers are a class 1 finance table, and deciding the care before reading is setting the class before the run.
samajh.boundary: Even the quick glance still counts the notes: every class still aligns the basis and compares keys, and only the depth beyond that changes.

beats.hint: Decide what a wrong number would cost before you look.

handbook.markdown:
**Why classes.** Reconciliation costs compute, time and owner attention. Spending the same on an exploration table as on the finance close either wastes effort or under-tests the close. A class set before the run, by the consequence of a wrong number, lets depth vary without letting anyone choose the depth after seeing the result.

**What never varies.** Every class writes the basis first (population, window, business-day rule, time zone, corrections, as-of time) and compares keys, because a matching total can hide keyed differences that cancel. The Reconciliation plan field guide holds that method; this matrix only sets depth.

**What varies.**
- *Field coverage*: every field (class 1), fields used by reports (class 2), key fields (class 3).
- *Tolerances*: exact for keys and integer sums in every class; a tolerance for rounded rates or floating values only when stated before the run, with a reason and an owner.
- *Parallel-run length*: long enough to include the workload's cycle; a month-end close needs a month-end.
- *Performance*: replay recorded queries at recorded concurrency against an agreed percentile target.
- *Permissions*: the persona matrix at the depth the class needs.
- *Sign-off*: who may accept residual differences.

**Worked example (synthetic).** The plant-quality mart is class 2: five consecutive clean days on every key and every reported field, exact integer totals, rates compared after rounding to two decimals, a 10-second p95 replay target for its dashboards, and the plant supervisors' personas tested. It is on day 3 of 5; a difference on day 4 would restart the count after the fix.

**When a class is wrong.** The failure to watch is a class drifting downward under schedule pressure; changing a class needs the business owner's written agreement, recorded with the reason.

**What to inspect.** The date each class was assigned, the tolerance list and who approved it, and the clean-day counter.

beats.recap: Set the class by consequence before the run; basis and keys never vary, depth does.

beats.title: Waves are ordered by dependencies and evidence, not by size
beats.outcome: Order migration waves around dependencies, fixed blackouts and exit tests, and re-plan when a wave slips.
beats.explanation: A [[dbxfe-warehouse-migration-wave-concept|wave]] is a set of workloads that cut over together, with entry conditions and an exit test. Notice in the first state that ordering by size puts the sensor cluster first, stranding the dashboards' line_health, and pushes finance into the year-end blackout. The second state orders by dependencies and evidence: foundations, the plant-quality pilot, the sensor cluster, finance after the close, then decommissioning. The third state shows a two-week slip in wave 1: wave 2 moves with it, but the blackout stays fixed.
beats.hint: Which dates can move, and which cannot?

handbook.markdown:
**What a wave is.** A group of workloads that cut over together, chosen so that few dependencies cross between waves and every crossing is bridged. Each wave has entry conditions (foundations ready, owners named, bridges built) and an exit test (its reconciliation class met, rollback rehearsed, consumers switched). AWS's wave-planning guidance makes the same moves in its own terms: group dependent workloads, confirm target design and ownership, rehearse cutover, and include validation and operational readiness.

**Ordering rules.**
1. *Wave 0 builds what every wave needs*: identities and groups, catalogs and grants, network paths, the reconciliation harness and the persona tests. No workload moves in wave 0.
2. *The pilot comes early*, chosen by the Migration inventory guide's criteria: bounded, representative of a hard feature, a reconciliation basis, an available owner and a reversible read path.
3. *Producers before consumers*, or a bridge for every cut edge.
4. *Blackouts are fixed*: a close, a peak season or an audit window moves waves, never the other way round.
5. *Decommissioning is a wave*: read-only first, then off after the recovery windows and the owners' acceptance.

**Re-planning a slip.** When wave 1 slipped two weeks, wave 2 moved with it because it reuses the pilot's patterns, leaving no slack before the blackout. The steering group, not the migration team, chooses between descoping wave 2 and accepting the risk, and the decision is recorded with its date.

**Cost of coexistence.** Every month of overlap runs two platforms and their bridges; the well-architected framework weighs cost alongside reliability, security and interoperability, so a dated end belongs in the plan.

**What to inspect.** Each wave's entry and exit tests, the bridges that span it and the buffer before each blackout.

beats.recap: Order waves by dependencies and fixed blackouts, give each an exit test, and let the owners decide on slips.

beats.title: Coexistence needs one writer per dataset and an end date
beats.outcome: Draw a coexistence architecture with one authoritative writer per dataset and a dated end for every bridge.
beats.explanation: During migration both platforms run, and the danger is two copies that both accept changes. The [[dbxfe-warehouse-migration-writer-concept|one-writer rule]] names, for each dataset at each moment, the single path allowed to write it; every other copy is derived and read-only. Notice in the first state that Basalt writes the quality mart during the parallel run while the lakehouse copy is compared, not edited. The second state flips the writer at cutover and adds a sync-back for finance; the third ends every [[dbxfe-warehouse-migration-bridge-concept|bridge]] and leaves Basalt read-only.

samajh.text: Salary account naye bank mein shift karte waqt kuch mahine dono account chalte hain. Har EMI kis account se katega, yeh ek hi account tay karta hai, dono nahi. Purane account mein ek standing instruction se paisa daalte rehte ho jab tak aakhri EMI shift na ho jaye, aur purana account tabhi band karte ho jab uska aakhri statement saaf aa jaye.
samajh.mapping: The two accounts are the two platforms, the account that pays each EMI is the dataset's single writer, the standing instruction is the sync-back, and closing the account is decommissioning.
samajh.boundary: A bank statement shows every transfer, while a data copy can drift silently; reconciliation has to produce the statement that a bank gives for free.

beats.hint: Who is allowed to write this dataset today?

handbook.markdown:
**The rule.** At any moment each dataset has exactly one authoritative writer. Every other copy is derived from it, read-only to users and reconciled against it. Corrections go to the writer, never to a copy, and the copy is rebuilt. HDFS applies the same idea to a single file (one writer at a time); coexistence applies it to whole datasets across platforms.

**Three phases for one dataset.**
1. *Parallel run*: the old platform writes and serves users; the new path runs on the same inputs and is compared daily.
2. *After cutover*: the new path writes and serves; if consumers remain on the old platform, a sync-back copies the new data there, read-only, and is reconciled daily.
3. *Exit*: the last consumer moves, the sync-back stops, and the old copy becomes a read-only archive until the recovery window ends.

**Architecture pieces.** Forward paths into the target (copies, file transfers, federated reads, which are read-only), backward paths out of it (sync-backs), the reconciliation job, BI routing (which reports read where) and the identity mapping. Each path has an owner, a freshness target and an end date.

**Worked example (synthetic).** In wave 1 Basalt writes the quality mart until cutover; afterwards the lakehouse writes it and syncs back to Basalt for the finance marts until wave 3. Pellworth coexists by decision, not by delay: its federation is reviewed once a year.

**What fails.** A user edits the new copy during the parallel run, and the next comparison reports a difference that is really a second writer. A sync-back without an end date becomes permanent. A bridge nobody owns stops silently.

**When not to coexist.** When the old platform cannot be kept consistent even read-only, or two platforms cost more than the risk they reduce; then a shorter, rehearsed cutover is better.

**What to inspect.** The writer for each dataset today, every path's end date, and whether any user can still write to a derived copy.

beats.recap: One writer per dataset at every moment; every bridge has an owner and an end.

beats.title: Pilot, parallel run, cutover, rollback: every step ends in a test
beats.outcome: Write the exit test for each step from pilot to recovery window and the triggers that start a rollback.
beats.explanation: Each step changes who depends on the new path, so each ends in a test rather than a date. Notice the states in order: the pilot proves the path for one plant while users stay on Basalt; the [[dbxfe-warehouse-migration-parallel-concept|parallel run]] compares both paths daily until the class's clean-day count is met; cutover switches users while Basalt keeps running as a named fallback; a written [[dbxfe-warehouse-migration-rollback-concept|rollback trigger]] returns them within a rehearsed time; and nothing is deleted until the recovery window ends and the owners accept.
beats.hint: What would make each step finished, and who checks it?

handbook.markdown:
**Pilot.** Prove the new path on real data for a bounded slice while users stay on the old path. Exit test: keyed reconciliation and persona tests pass for the slice and the owner accepts the differences found. A pilot that only proves the code runs has not ended.

**Parallel run.** Run both paths on the same inputs for the whole wave, compare daily at the wave's risk class and count clean days. A fix restarts the count; days before it are not carried forward. Exit test: the class's clean-day count, a performance replay and a rehearsed rollback.

**Cutover.** A decision, not a date. Entry conditions are written so a named person can verify each one: the clean days and the exception register, the persona test, the rehearsal record, a named operator and backup, and users told where the fallback is. The old path keeps running, renamed as the fallback, so nobody mistakes it for the new one.

**Rollback.** Triggers are observable and written in advance: the report not ready by a stated time, a difference beyond the accepted exceptions, an access anomaly. Any one is enough; the operator reverts first and diagnoses second, and users are told which day's data they saw from which path. Rehearse it before cutover against a time target and record what the rehearsal found. The retained lesson on reconciliation and rollback covers data written after the switch.

**Recovery window and cleanup.** Nothing on the old side is deleted until the window ends without a trigger and the owners accept the cleanup. AWS's pre-cutover guidance names the same ingredients: dependencies, rehearsal, rollback, testing and an ordered runbook with owners and times.

**Worked numbers (synthetic).** Pilot: plant 1 for one week. Parallel run: all plants at class 2, five clean days, with day 4 failing once and restarting the count. Rehearsed rollback: 20 minutes against a 30-minute target. Recovery window: 20 working days.

**What to inspect.** Each step's exit test, the trigger list, the rehearsal record and the cleanup acceptance.

beats.recap: Pilot, parallel run, cutover, rollback, recovery window: each ends in a written test, never a date.

extensionCards.prompt: What do Lakebridge's reconcile report types compare, and what do they leave unproven?
extensionCards.answer: In release 0.15.2, schema reports compare column definitions, data reports join on configured keys and row reports join on whole-row hashes; none proves the basis, performance or permissions.
extensionCards.explanation: Reading the 0.15.2 package shows the mechanics. A data [[dbxfe-warehouse-migration-extension-reconcile-concept|report type]] full-joins source and target on the key columns you configure and returns mismatched rows, rows missing in the source and rows missing in the target, keeping up to 50 sample rows per set by default, with optional thresholds on chosen columns. A row report joins on a hash of each whole row instead, so a changed row appears as one row missing on each side and cannot be told apart from a replaced key. A schema report compares column definitions, and 'all' combines schema and data. The commands are labelled experimental, the package is classified Beta and the README offers no formal support. The comparison is only as good as the basis aligned before it, and timing and permission outcomes need their own tests.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: Tells you exactly what a tool-generated reconciliation proves, so its output is used as evidence at the right depth rather than as a verdict.

extensionCards.prompt: Why can very old dates read differently after a Spark 2.4 estate moves to Spark 3 or later?
extensionCards.answer: Spark 3.0 replaced the hybrid Julian and Gregorian calendar with the Proleptic Gregorian calendar, which changes dates before 15 October 1582.
extensionCards.explanation: Spark 2.4 and earlier computed dates with a hybrid calendar: Julian before 15 October 1582 and Gregorian after it. Since 3.0, Spark uses the [[dbxfe-warehouse-migration-extension-calendar-concept|Proleptic Gregorian calendar]] throughout, based on Java's java.time classes, so a stored day number written by an older engine can mean a different date when a newer one reads it. Spark's migration guide documents rebase settings for Parquet and Avro reads and writes, and in 4.0 those settings lost their spark.sql.legacy prefix. In a manufacturing estate this matters for placeholder dates such as 0001-01-01 used to mean 'unknown': list the columns that hold such values and compare them after the move.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: Sentinel and historical dates can shift silently in a Hadoop migration; knowing the mechanism tells you which columns to compare.

extensionCards.prompt: What does Microsoft Fabric's mirroring add to a coexistence design, and what does it leave unchanged?
extensionCards.answer: It continuously replicates data from sources such as Azure Databricks or Snowflake into OneLake, but it is still a lagging copy whose writer stays upstream.
extensionCards.explanation: Microsoft's Fabric overview says [[dbxfe-warehouse-migration-extension-mirroring-concept|mirroring]] continuously replicates an existing data estate into OneLake, naming sources including Azure SQL Database, Azure Cosmos DB, Azure Databricks, Snowflake and Fabric SQL database, and that shortcuts give zero-copy access to ADLS, Amazon S3 and Google Cloud Storage. For a coexistence design this means a Fabric-based consumer can be supplied in either direction without a hand-built export. The rules do not change: a mirror is a replicated copy with a lag, its writer stays upstream, and keyed reconciliation and persona outcomes still have to be proven on the side users read. Check the current source list and preview labels on Microsoft's own pages before relying on a particular source.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: Shows that other platforms provide their own movement options, and that the one-writer and reconciliation rules apply whichever vendor makes the copy.

extensionCards.prompt: How do Redshift row-level security and dynamic masking policies translate into Unity Catalog?
extensionCards.answer: Each policy's intent becomes a row filter or a column mask, and a persona test proves the outcomes match; the policy syntax does not carry over.
extensionCards.explanation: AWS's archived Redshift developer guide describes [[dbxfe-warehouse-migration-extension-policies-concept|row-level security policies]] that restrict the rows users or roles can access, and dynamic data masking that transforms sensitive values at query time; roles can inherit permissions from other roles, and permissions start with the object owner. Unity Catalog's row filters and column masks are also query-time controls, evaluated for the principal that runs the query. Translate intent: list each policy, the principals it targets and its predicate or masking rule, write the equivalent filter or mask, and run the persona matrix for every role in an inheritance chain, because flattening roles into groups can add or remove access. AWS's live row-level security page adds that RLS policies apply to SELECT, UPDATE and DELETE but not to INSERT, COPY or ALTER TABLE APPEND, so the matrix must include the write statements each persona may run, not only reads. The archived details are out of date since 2023, so check the live pages for the options Pellworth actually uses.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: Pellworth's finance data depends on these policies; mapping them by intent and proving them by outcome is what keeps coexistence or a later move safe.

recap.title: Readers, dispositions, bridges and proof
recap.markdown: **Inventory by readers, segment by workload, and give each workload one disposition, one driver and the evidence that would make it agreed.** Every dependency a wave boundary cuts needs a bridge with an owner and an end. Profile each source platform in its own vendor's words and leave unread cells unknown. Silent dialect and engine differences, not loud ones, carry the risk, and conversion tools measure syntax: results, performance and permissions each need their own proof, at a depth set before the run by the consequence of a wrong number. Waves follow dependencies and fixed blackouts, coexistence keeps one writer per dataset, and pilot, parallel run, cutover and rollback each end in a written test. **Transfer challenge:** redo Cinderline's segmentation for the case where Pellworth runs Microsoft Fabric instead of Redshift, and mark which profile cells Microsoft's overview answers and which stay unknown with an owner.

appliedTask.title: Plan Pellworth's move after its review
appliedTask.prompt: A year later, Pellworth's security review approves moving its finance mart from Amazon Redshift into Cinderline's lakehouse. The mart uses row-level security policies for plant managers, dynamic masking on supplier prices, three roles of which one inherits from another, 40 dashboards on live queries, and feeds a month-end close. Today it is federated read-only. Plan the move: data movement during and after the transition, the security mapping and its proof, BI continuity, the reconciliation class and parallel-run length, and the rollback triggers.
appliedTask.modelAnswer: Data movement: replace federation with an initial copy and nightly incremental loads, with Pellworth as the single writer until cutover; after cutover the lakehouse writes and the 40 dashboards read it. Security: list every row-level security policy, masking policy and role with its principals and rule; express them as row filters, column masks and group grants; run the persona matrix for every role, including the inherited one, before and after flattening roles into groups. BI: move measures and rules into one governed definition, map refresh identities to service principals, and compare totals per plant and day. Validation: class 1, every key and field, one full month-end close in parallel. Rollback triggers: close figures not ready by the agreed time, a keyed difference outside the exception register, or an access anomaly; rehearse the switch back before cutover and keep Redshift read-only until the recovery window ends.
appliedTask.reasoning: The answer changes the movement option because a migration needs a copy with a single writer, maps policies by intent and proves them by persona outcomes, and sets class 1 depth because the close involves money.
